claims.text: NbTaTiV is an example of a BCC refractory high-entropy alloy relevant to the proposed test.
The experiment starts from an as-manufactured, single-phase BCC alloy with a baseline dislocation microstructure and minimal prior thermomechanical conditioning.
Elevated-temperature thermoelastic and mechanical responses in refractory BCC HEAs are primarily governed by edge-dislocation mobility and density evolution.
Local lattice distortions induce the proposed evolution of edge-dislocation mobility and density.
Minor interstitial segregation induces the proposed evolution of edge-dislocation mobility and density.
Edge-dislocation density and spatial distribution are modulated by local lattice distortions and interstitial segregation.
Short-range order and local lattice distortions enhance edge-dislocation mobility at high temperature.
Edge dislocations can predominantly control high-temperature strength and plastic flow in NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV refractory HEAs.
Edge-dislocation mobility predominantly controls the elastic moduli and thermoelastic response of refractory BCC HEAs.
Conventional elemental BCC metals and dilute BCC alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations during plastic flow.
Thermomechanical pre-conditioning at 800–1200 °C will increase edge-dislocation density relative to the as-received baseline.
The increased edge-dislocation density will be spatially correlated with shifts in lattice-strain evolution and elastic moduli.
In situ neutron diffraction can measure elevated-temperature lattice-strain evolution and obtain elastic moduli in a single-phase BCC refractory HEA.
Microscopy coupled with diffraction can distinguish the role of edge dislocations from that of screw dislocations.
A single BCC solid-solution phase can remain stable during elevated-temperature testing up to at least 900 °C.
The single-phase BCC assumption remains applicable throughout the full proposed range of 800–1200 °C.
High temperature and changes in strain rate can introduce grain-boundary slip or alter which deformation mechanism dominates.
Screw dislocations may contribute substantially or dominate in some BCC refractory HEAs.
Holding composition fixed isolates lattice-distortion effects.

The hypothesis is falsified if edge-dislocation density does not increase, elastic moduli do not change in correlation with edge density, and screw dislocations or another mechanism dominate under the designated conditions.
